newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal labour mkt robust, no inflation tensions.
newsitem.headline: Portugal labour mkt robust, no inflation tensions.

text.p: Portugal's labour market is robust and reflects a quickening in economic growth, but inflationary tensions are not on the horizon, analysts said.

They said that even with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth at slightly above three percent, and despite disappointing May inflation data, the average annual inflation rate could well hold out at below the government's maximum goal of 2.5 percent.

Last Friday, the National Statistics Institute (INE) announced a sharp drop in second quarter unemployment to 6.5 percent from 7.3 percent in the first quarter and 7.2 percent in the second quarter of 1996.
In the second quarter, the number of employees was 4.335 million, up from 4.246 million in the same period of 1996.
The increase in employment levels was due mainly to job creation in agriculture and construction, INE said.
"The drop in unemployment is quicker than had been expected and confirms that the economy is growing at a dynamic rhythm," said Jose Luis Alzola, analyst of Salomon Brothers in London.
"Perhaps we will have to revise upwards our estimates for 1997 GDP growth to 3.3 percent from 3.1 percent," he added.

Nuno Godinho, analyst of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon, said: "The latest indicators point to a drastic reduction in unemployment and a poor inflation result for May, but there are no reasons for alarm as both the fall in unemployment and the rise in inflation are exceptional."

In May, the consumer price index rose 0.7 percent, putting the year-on-year rate at 2.1 percent and the average annual rate at 3.0 percent, compared with a monthly increase of 0.2 percent, a year-on-year rate of 1.8 percent and an average annual rate of 3.1 percent in April.
The high May inflation figure was explained in part by large increases in pork and potato prices.
"If you strip out the more volatile elements (above all, food prices), the rise in May inflation was not significant," said Alzola.

Isabel Cabral, analyst of Lisbon broker Fincor, said: "Economic growth in 1997 should be slightly above three percent, and that is quite compatible with an average inflation rate of nearer 2.0 than 2.5 percent."
Godinho said: "Given the moderation in wage rises that we have seen this year, salaries will not create inflationary problems."
From January to May 1997 wage inflation in the private sector stood at 3.6 percent, 0.9 percentage points below the same year-ago period, INE said.
Alzola said he had revised downwards his forecasts for unemployment in Portugal in 1997 to an average rate of 6.6 or 6.7 percent from 6.9 or 7.0 percent previously.
He said that at that level, unemployment would not create inflationary tensions in Portugal.
Cabral underlined her optimism that inflation would stay low as consumer spending had not been behind the large May increase.

Between February and April, car sales fell 2.1 percent year-on-year, INE said. In the first quarter, petrol sales rose by 0.8 percent, compared with 3.5 percent in the last quarter of 1996. Sales in supermarkets rose 6.7 pct in the first quarter, compared with 9.8 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.

Cabral said that if GDP growth rose as high as 3.75 percent this year, inflation would reach uncomfortable levels. But she said it was unlikely that the economy would grow so fast as consumer spending remained subdued.
